note.text: This guided classroom comparison applies the earlier lessons. Ownership, liability, finance, control and continuity are separate criteria. The best fit depends on the case’s priorities and constraints, not the biggest-sounding name. A form can solve one problem while creating another: pooled funds may require shared control, and liability protection can involve greater formality. A cooperative is introduced here as member-owned and democratically controlled; later lessons examine it more fully. No actual business is registered in this exercise.

sections.heading: Your goal and connections
sections.text: By the end, you should be able to choose a defensible form for a fictional case and explain a trade-off rather than naming a universal winner. Builds on: sole ownership, partnerships and company identity. Leads to: cooperative study and the later locality business-planning case.

sections.heading: Understand the economics
sections.text: This guided classroom comparison applies the earlier lessons. Ownership, liability, finance, control and continuity are separate criteria. The best fit depends on the case’s priorities and constraints, not the biggest-sounding name. A form can solve one problem while creating another: pooled funds may require shared control, and liability protection can involve greater formality. A cooperative is introduced here as member-owned and democratically controlled; later lessons examine it more fully. No actual business is registered in this exercise.

sections.heading: Follow the local case
sections.text: Fictional cases compare a Buea repair stall, a Bamenda workshop with complementary partners, a Douala company seeking equity and a group of growers seeking shared services. The same commercial activity can use different legal forms. Learners should read the ownership and purpose described rather than decide that all farms or shops have one form.

sections.heading: Reason and check
sections.text: Make a comparison sheet with ownership, decision method, finance and an important limitation. State a choice, cite a case fact and acknowledge a cost. If legal feasibility or actual demand is unknown, list what needs checking instead of inventing a guarantee.
